'''Jerzy Spława-Neyman''' (also known as '''Jerzy Neyman'''; {{IPA|pl|ˈjɛʐɨ ˈspwava ˈnɛjman|pron}}; April 16, 1894 – August 5, 1981) was a Polish [[mathematician]] and [[statistician]]. He made major contributions to the development of modern [[statistical theory]].<ref name="Brit">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jerzy-Neyman |title=Jerzy Neyman |website=Encyclopaedia Britannica |publisher=Britannica |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> Neyman introduced the modern concept of a [[confidence interval]] into [[statistical hypothesis testing]]<ref name="tea">{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9Q0EDh43cxYC&pg=PA123 | title=The Lady Tasting Tea: How Statistics Revolutionized Science in the Twentieth Century | publisher=Macmillan | author=Salsburg, David | year=2002 | pages=122 | isbn=9780805071344}}</ref> and, with [[Egon Pearson]], revised [[Ronald Fisher]]'s [[null hypothesis]] testing. [[Neyman allocation]], an optimal strategy for choosing sample sizes in [[stratified sampling]], is named for him.

He spent the first part of his professional career at various institutions in [[Warsaw]], [[Poland]], and then at [[University College London]], and the second part at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] where he founded and developed one of the world’s leading centres of [[mathematical statistics]]. 

Neyman was the recipient of many awards during his career including the [[Guy Medal]], the [[Newcomb Cleveland Prize]], and the [[National Medal of Science]]. He was a member of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]], the [[Polish Mathematical Society]], the [[National Academy of Sciences]], and [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].

==Life and career==
===Early life and education===
Neyman was born on 16 April 1894 into a [[Polish people|Polish]] family in [[Bendery]], in the [[Bessarabia Governorate]] of the [[Russian Empire]] (present-day [[Bender, Moldova|Bender]], Moldova), the fourth of four children of Czesław Spława-Neyman, a lawyer,<ref name="MacTut">{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Neyman/ |title=Jerzy Neyman |website=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive|author=J. J. O'Connor, E. F. Robertson |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sejm-wielki.pl/b/psb.31232.2 |language=pl |title=Czesław Neyman-Spława h. Spława |website=sejm-wielki,pl |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> and Kazimiera ([[née]] Lutosławska).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sejm-wielki.pl/b/psb.31232.3 |language=pl |title=Kazimiera Lutosławska |website=sejm-wielki,pl |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> His family was [[Roman Catholic]] and descended from a long line of Polish nobles and military heroes. Neyman served as an [[Altar server|altar boy]] during his early childhood, though he would become an agnostic in later life. By the time he was 10, he could speak five languages: [[Polish language|Polish]], [[Ukrainian language|Ukrainian]], [[Russian language|Russian]], [[French language|French]] and [[German language|German]].<ref name="MacTut"></ref> 

He graduated from the [[Kamianets-Podilskyi|Kamieniec Podolski]] gubernial [[gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]] for boys in 1909 under the name ''Yuri Cheslavovich Neyman''.<ref>[http://zhurnal.lib.ru/k/kitlinskij_a_a/gimnazij.shtml Выпускники Каменец-Подольской гимназии 1883-1920]</ref> Neyman's father died of [[heart attack]] when he was 12<ref name="Amstat">{{cite web|url=https://magazine.amstat.org/blog/2017/04/13/sih-neyman/ |title=Jerzy Neyman |website=magazine.amstat.org |date=13 April 2017 |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> and his family subsequently relocated to [[Kharkiv]].<ref name="Domański">{{cite web|url=https://ws.stat.gov.pl/WS/2021/12/gus_ws_2021_12_czeslaw_domanski_poczatki_tworczosci_naukowej_jerzego_splawy-neymana.pdf |language=pl |title=Początki twórczości naukowej Jerzego Spławy-Neymana  |trans-title=The Beginnings of the scientific Career of Jerzy Spława-Neyman |work=Wiadomości Statystyczne |author=Czesław Domański |date=7 July 2021 |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> He began studies at [[Kharkiv University]] in 1912, where he was taught by Ukrainian probabilist [[Sergei Natanovich Bernstein]], who exerted an enduring influence on him. Neyman was not drafted into the army following the outbreak of [[World War I]] due to poor eyesight, which enabled him to stay at the university and continue his education.<ref name="MacTut"></ref> 

After having read ''Lessons on the integration and the research of the primitive functions'' by [[Henri Lebesgue]], he was fascinated with [[measure theory]] and integration. In 1915, he completed a paper on Lebesgue integration for which he was awarded Gold Medal.<ref name="MacTut"></ref> In 1917–21, he worked as an assiatant of Antoni Przeborski at the Technological Institute in Kharkiv.<ref name="Wójcik"></ref> 

In the period of the [[Russian Revolution]], Neyman's health began to deteriorate. Doctors diagnosed [[tuberculosis]], advising him to travel south to recuperate. In 1919, he went to the [[Crimea]], where he met a Russian woman, Olga Solodovnikova, who was a painter.<ref name="Domański"></ref> Soon after he returned to Kharkov to begin teaching in the autumn of that year, Olga also came back, and their friendship eventually led to their marriage in 1920.<ref name="MacTut"></ref>

===Professional career===
In 1921, Neyman returned to [[Poland]] in a program of repatriation of [[POW]]s after the [[Polish-Soviet War]].<ref name="Amstat"></ref> He briefly worked at the Institute of Agricultural Reseach in [[Bydgoszcz]].<ref name="Wójcik"></ref> His first scientific paper ''Sur un théorème métrique, concernant les ensembles fermés'' was published in 1923 in ''[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]]''.<ref name="Domański"></ref> During his student years, Neyman devoted much of his limited free time to teaching mathematics and statistics, including to college students, in order to support himself.<ref name="Amstat"></ref> In 1924, he earned his [[doctorate]] at [[University of Warsaw]] for a dissertation titled ''Justification of Applications of Calculus of Probability to the Solution of Certain Questions of Agricultural Experimentation'' written under the supervision of [[Wacław Sierpiński]].<ref name="MathGen">{{cite web|url=https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=12694 |title=Jerzy Neyman |work=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref><!-- names to be moved to a trivia section with explication that his exams did not concerned statistics-->.  

After having been granted the [[Fund for National Culture (Poland)|Fund for National Culture]] and [[Rockefeller Foundation]] scholarships, in 1924–26, he stayed in London, where he collaborated with [[Karl Pearson]], his son [[Egon Pearson|Egon]], and [[Ronald Fisher]] and in Paris, where he attended lectures by [[Henri Lebesgue]] and [[Émile Borel]], and a seminar by [[Jacques Hadamard]] at the [[Collège de France]].<ref name="Wójcik"></ref><ref name="Domański"></ref><ref name="Amstat"></ref>

His work with Egon Pearson proved especially fruitful as the two authored six joint papers between 1926–34 including "On the Problem of Two Samples" published by the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] (1930)<ref name="MacTut"></ref> and "On the Problem of the Most Efficient Tests of Statistical Hypotheses" (1933), which contained the [[Neyman-Pearson lemma]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsta/article/231/694-706/289/40532/IX-On-the-problem-of-the-most-efficient-tests-of?utm_source=copilot.com |title=IX. On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses |author=Jerzy Neyman, Egon Pearson |journal=The Royal Society Publishing |date=1933 |volume=231 |issue=694–706 |pages=289–337 |doi=10.1098/rsta.1933.0009 |bibcode=1933RSPTA.231..289N |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> 
[[File:Jerzy Neyman.jpg|thumb|Neyman in Warsaw, 1973]]
After his return to Poland, he established the Biometric Laboratory at the [[Nencki Institute of Experimental Biology]] in Warsaw. In 1923–34, he served as director of the Statistical Laboratory of the [[Warsaw University of Life Sciences]] (SGGW).<ref name="Wójcik">{{cite web|url=https://gigancinauki.pl/gn/biogramy/84142,Splawa-Neyman-Jerzy.html |language=pl |title=Spława-Neyman Jerzy |website=gigancinauki |author=Wiesław Wójcik |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> In 1928, Neyman obtained [[habilitation]] at the SGGW. In 1934, at Egon Pearson’s invitation, he travelled to Britain, where he lectured at [[University College London]]. During his tenure at University College, Neyman wrote a paper on [[stratified sampling]] that helped establish the methodological basis for what became the [[Gallup Poll]].<ref name="NatMed"></ref> 

Neyman proposed and studied randomized experiments in 1923.<ref>Neyman, Jerzy. 1923 [1990]. “On the Application of Probability Theory to Agricultural Experiments. Essay on Principles. Section 9.” ''Statistical Science'' 5 (4): 465–472. Trans. [[Dorota Dabrowska|Dorota M. Dabrowska]] and Terence P. Speed.
</ref> His paper "On the Two Different Aspects of the Representative Method: The Method of [[Stratified sampling|Stratified Sampling]] and the Method of Purposive Selection", given at the [[Royal Statistical Society]] on 19 June 1934,<ref>Neyman, J.(1934) "On the two different aspects of the representative method: The method of stratified sampling and the method of purposive selection", ''[[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]]'', 97 (4), 557–625 {{JSTOR|2342192}}</ref> was the groundbreaking event leading to modern scientific sampling. He introduced the [[confidence interval]] in his paper in 1937.<ref name="Ney">{{Cite journal | last1=Neyman | first1=Jerzy | title=Outline of a Theory of Statistical Estimation Based on the Classical Theory of Probability | year=1937  | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences | volume=236 | issue=767 | pages=333–380| doi=10.1098/rsta.1937.0005 | jstor=91337| bibcode=1937RSPTA.236..333N | doi-access=free }}</ref> 

He was an Invited Speaker of the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] (ICM) in 1928 in [[Bologna]]<ref>{{cite book|author=Neyman, J.|chapter=On methods of testing hypotheses|title=''In:'' Atti del Congresso Internazionale dei Matematici: Bologna del 3 al 10 de settembre di 1928|volume=6|pages=35–42}}</ref> and a Plenary Speaker of the ICM in 1954 in [[Amsterdam]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Neyman, J.|chapter=Probabilistic theory of clustering of galaxies with particular reference to the hypothesis of an expanding universe|title=''In:'' Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians: Amsterdam, 1954|volume=2|pages=298–299|year=1954}}</ref> In 1929, at the 18th session of the [[International Statistical Institute]] held in Warsaw, Neyman delivered a talk entitled "A Contribution to the Theory of the Credibility of Statistical Hypotheses."<ref name="Domański"></ref>

In 1937, he visited the United States and spent six weeks giving lectures at a number of univeristies, including the Graduate School in the U.S. Department of Agriculture in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]],<ref name="Amstat"></ref> in which he spoke about the importance of [[probability theory]] to [[statistics]], developing his theories and presenting his research findings to support it. Based on these lectures, Neyman published a book in 1938 entitled ''Lectures and Conferences on Mathematical Statistics''.<ref name="Wójcik"></ref> He also published books dealing with experiments and statistics, and devised the way which the [[Food and Drug Administration]] tests medicines today.

===Move to the United States===
[[File:Wheeler Hall, University of California, Berkeley.jpg|thumb|Neyman spent his academic career in the United States at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].]]
In 1938, Neyman moved to [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]], where he worked for the rest of his life at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="MacTut"></ref> After the outbreak of [[World War II]], he briefly turned to military research focusing in particular on bomb‑sight design and targeting problems. During his time at Berkeley, he sought to establish a world‑class centre for mathematical statistics at this institution, working relentlessly toward this aim<ref name="MacTut"></ref> advancing concepts in estimation and hypothesis‑testing theory.<ref name="NatMed"></ref> He established there the Statistical Laboratory, a scientific center which worked for many institutions including the [[Federal government of the United States|U.S. government]].<ref name="Wójcik"></ref> His efforts culminated in the creation of a separate statistics department at the university on 1 July 1955.<ref name="MacTut"></ref>

Throughout his academic career, 45 students obtained their PhD degrees under his advisorship including [[George Dantzig]], [[Lucien Le Cam]], [[Evelyn Fix]], [[Erich Leo Lehmann]], [[Joseph Lawson Hodges, Jr.|Joseph Hodges]], [[Pao-Lu Hsu]], and [[Frank J. Massey]].<ref name="MathGen"></ref>

===Recognition and death===
Neyman was a recipient of many prestigious awards for his contributions to science. In 1958, he was awarded the [[Newcomb Cleveland Prize]] of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS). In 1966, he received the [[Guy Medal]] of the [[Royal Statistical Society]] and, three years later, he accepted the U.S. [[National Medal of Science]], the highest science award in the [[United States]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=About the National Medal of Science |url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/about.jsp |access-date=21 September 2026 |website=www.nsf.gov |date=14 July 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-11 |title=President Biden awards National Medal of Science to Brown engineer Subra Suresh |url=https://www.brown.edu/news/2023-10-24/suresh-medal-science |access-date=21 September 2026 |website=www.brown.edu |language=en}}</ref> from [[President of the United States|President]] [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] "for laying the foundations of modern statistics and devising tests and procedure that have become essential parts of the knowledge of every statistician."<ref name="NatMed">{{cite web|url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/jerzy-neyman/ |title=Jerzy Neyman |work=National Medal of Science |access-date=21 September 2026}}</ref> He died in [[Oakland, California|Oakland]], [[California]], in 1981.<ref name="MacTut"></ref>

==Contributions==
Neyman’s scholarly output comprises more than 240 publications, covering an exceptionally broad range of topics – from pure [[mathematical statistics]], the theory of [[stochastic processe]]s, and [[Sampling (statistics)|sampling theory]] to applications in [[agriculture]], [[epidemiology]], [[meteorology]], [[genetics]], [[biology]], [[medical diagnosis]], [[social insurance]], and [[astronomy]].<ref name="Wójcik"></ref><ref name="Brit"></ref><ref name="MacTut"></ref>

Neyman played a central role in shaping modern [[hypothesis testing]]. In 1933, together with Egon Pearson, he introduced the concept in statistics known as the [[Neyman-Pearson lemma]], which asserts the existence and uniqueness of the likelihood ratio as a [[uniformly most powerful test]] in specified settings.<ref name="np1933">{{Cite journal |last1=Neyman |first1=J. |last2=Pearson|first2=E. S. |date=1933-02-16 |title=IX. On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses |journal=Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A |language=en |volume=231|issue=694–706 |pages=289–337 |doi=10.1098/rsta.1933.0009 |bibcode=1933RSPTA.231..289N |issn=0264-3952 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It forms a central component of the broader Neyman–Pearson theory for statistical testing, which also developed key notions such as [[Type II error]], [[power (statistics)|power function]], and inductive behavior.<ref>The Fisher, Neyman–Pearson Theories of Testing Hypotheses: One Theory or Two?: Journal of the American Statistical Association: Vol 88, No 424: [https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1993.10476404 The Fisher, Neyman–Pearson Theories of Testing Hypotheses: One Theory or Two?: Journal of the American Statistical Association: Vol 88, No 424]</ref><ref>Wald: Chapter II: The Neyman–Pearson Theory of Testing a Statistical Hypothesis: [https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ndml/1175196981 Wald: Chapter II: The Neyman–Pearson Theory of Testing a Statistical Hypothesis]</ref>

A key part of Neyman's collaboration with Pearson was a systematic revision of [[Ronald Fisher]]’s formulation of the [[null hypothesis]]. Fisher had emphasized significance testing as a measure of evidence against a null model, but Neyman and Pearson reframed the problem: instead of treating the null as something to be “rejected” or “not rejected,” they defined hypothesis testing as a decision procedure with controlled long‑run error probabilities.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lu |first=Xiao-Kang |year=2012 |title=The discrepancy between Fisher and Neyman–Pearson on hypothesis testing |journal=Journal of Probability and Statistics |volume=2012 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.1155/2012/263401 |doi-broken-date=21 September 2026 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Another significant contribution by Neyman was introduced in 1934, and is now known as the [[Neyman allocation]]. It is a [[stratified sampling|stratified‑sampling method]] which specifies the optimal sample size for each stratum so as to minimize the variance of an estimated population parameter given a fixed overall sample size and cost.

In 1937, Neyman developed the concept of the [[confidence interval]] into a general framework for [[statistical hypothesis test]]s.<ref name="Ney"></ref> In [[Frequentist inference|frequentist statistics]], it denotes a range of values that, under repeated sampling, is expected to contain the true value of an unknown parameter, for example, a population mean.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.21037/jtd.2017.09.14 | doi-access=free | title=Using the confidence interval confidently | date=2017 | last1=Hazra | first1=Avijit | journal=Journal of Thoracic Disease | volume=9 | issue=10 | pages=4124–4129 | pmid=29268424 | pmc=5723800 }}</ref> Other notalbe concepts named after Neyman include the [[Neyman construction]], [[Neyman Type A distribution]], [[Neyman–Scott process]], the [[Rubin causal model|Neyman-Rubin causal model]], and the [[Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem]].
